To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

vibrational-to-electron conversion efficiency is high, the electron kinetic energy distribution is broad, and the most probable kinetic energy is a large fraction (64%) of the initial vibrating energy.

vibrational energy of molecules can be converted into electronic energy of the surface with a remarkable efficiency, and that the energy transfer can be understood in terms of a simple model of vibrational excitation and relaxation of surface electrons.
vibrational-to-electron energy conversion is efficient and can occur in a single collision.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the dynamics of electron emission from metals by collisions with molecules and atoms.
the development of a novel, non-invasive, real time, in situ, and non-destructive method for the determination of the surface composition and morphology of a variety of materials.
the study of the vibrational excitation of molecules by electron collisions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vibrational-to-electron energy transfer is a very efficient process and that it can occur in a single collision event.
vibrational excitation is a very efficient means for producing electrons at a metal surface.
the vibrational energy is transferred to the electrons in the metal in a highly efficient manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the exoelectron emission process is a very efficient process for the conversion of the vibrational energy into electronic energy, and the electron kinetic energy is a very sensitive probe for the dynamics of this conversion.
vibrational energy is efficiently converted to electron excitations at a surface.

we have demonstrated the ability to measure the kinetic energy of the exoelectrons and that this kinetic energy is consistent with the vibrational energy of the molecule and the electron affinity of the metal surface.
The main takeaway from our work is that
vibrational energy is a useful resource for the generation of electrons at metal surfaces.
electron kinetic energy distribution can be a powerful tool in elucidating electron excitation mechanisms in molecular collision processes.

the electron emission probability is not a simple step function in electron energy but rather is a smooth function with a maximum at a kinetic energy of 0.6 eV and a full width at half maximum of 1.0 eV.
